analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial asbestos from manufacturing and commerce, phasing out its last major US use.
analysis.headline: A Democratic representative and one Republican cosponsor introduced the asbestos ban, and it has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing or vote since its September 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to manufacture, process, use, or sell commercial asbestos — all eight of its commercial forms — as soon as it became law. The handful of chlorine plants that still use asbestos would get until 2030 to switch to other technology, and the President could grant a national security exemption of up to six years when no alternative exists. Asbestos already installed in buildings would not be touched by the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in chlorine plants, brake and gasket factories, construction, and demolition — plus their families and the general public — gain protection from a known cause of mesothelioma and lung cancer. Asbestos exposure has no safe level, and the bill would cut off new commercial uses immediately and the largest remaining one (chlorine production) by 2030.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and the public exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits, effective on enactment, the manufacture, processing, use, and sale in commerce of commercial asbestos in any of its eight commercial forms, including chrysotile, the type still imported into the US.

Closes the largest remaining ongoing exposure channel: chlor-alkali plants that use asbestos to make chlorine would have to stop using and processing asbestos, and stop using asbestos diaphragms, by January 1, 2030.

Keeps the escape hatches narrow. The national security exemption requires the President to find that no feasible alternative exists, lasts at most three years with one three-year extension, and must be published in the Federal Register (with limited classified exceptions reported to Congress).
Prevents any backdoor loosening: it bars the EPA Administrator from waiving the prohibition, while leaving existing asbestos rules — such as FDA authority over asbestos in cosmetics — intact.

analysis.who_pays: The chlor-alkali industry — a small number of US chlorine plants that still use asbestos diaphragms — would have to pay to convert to asbestos-free membrane technology by 2030. Importers and makers of asbestos-containing products (gaskets, brake components, and similar goods) lose their product line immediately, and any transition costs could feed modestly into chlorine and product prices.

drawbacks.text: The chlor-alkali exemption lets plants keep using and processing asbestos for more than four years after enactment, so worker exposure at those facilities continues well past the ban's effective date.

The ban does not touch asbestos already installed in buildings, products, and equipment — the legacy asbestos that drives most exposure today — which the bill simply excludes from 'distribution in commerce' and requires to be disposed of under existing rules.

Asbestos present 'solely as an impurity' is carved out entirely, so products with trace contamination — such as talc-based goods — are not covered by this section, and the bill leaves cosmetics regulation to the FDA's existing, separate authority.

Converting chlorine plants off asbestos technology costs real money for the plants affected, and a national security exemption could in principle keep some use going for up to six years without full public disclosure of the terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gain is large relative to the cost. Only a small share of the US chlorine industry still uses asbestos — most plants already switched to asbestos-free membranes — so the conversion burden falls on a few facilities over a five-year window, while the ban would end new commercial asbestos uses outright. The honest caveats are timing: the main continuing use gets years of runway, and legacy asbestos already in place is left alone, so this is a phase-down of remaining exposures rather than an immediate end to them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on September 16, 2025, joined from the start by one Republican cosponsor, Rep. Bacon.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over toxic substances law.
Since that referral there have been no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill's entire history is two entries long.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so the status quo holds: the small group of chlorine plants still importing and using raw asbestos continues doing so, and no new protections exist for workers or the public.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plants still importing asbestos, for now

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to referral in the House.

for.name: Rep. Bacon
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its only cosponsor, making the introduction bipartisan.

sides.party_line_note: It is too early to call: one Republican cosponsor joined the Democratic sponsor, and no hearings or votes have revealed where either party stands.

industries.note: A handful of US chlorine plants still import raw chrysotile asbestos for the diaphragms used in production — the country's main remaining asbestos use. The bill gives these plants until January 1, 2030 to convert to asbestos-free technology, which most of their competitors have already done.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: The ban immediately prohibits making, processing, using, and selling commercial asbestos and mixtures or articles containing it, ending product lines such as asbestos-containing gaskets and friction products.
The bill leaves legacy asbestos in place and requires that any distribution be solely for compliant disposal, sustaining demand for professional removal and disposal work.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no hearing, and no committee action on a bill referred to Energy and Commerce, the likely path is the one similar asbestos-ban bills have taken in earlier Congresses: it sits in committee until the session ends without a markup or vote. Getting to the floor would require the committee's Republican majority to schedule it, which typically happens only with leadership support that does not exist here.
